    - - - - - - -

    A classic piece of surplus Great Britain. These lovely shirts were issued for a little over a decade and saw use in Iraq and the Gulf War. Made of a light poly-cotton material the shirt provides comfort and flexibility where needed. Officially these are combat jackets, but work just as well as a shirt!

    The jacket comes with 2 main chest pockets for storing slightly larger items and then a pen sleeve on the left with a small pocket on the right for whatever you may need. The jacket can be buttoned or zipped shut and if it's a particularly windy day the cuffs can be fastened tighter and collar overturned to provide better insulation.

    Desert Disruptive Pattern Material or DDPM, was developed in the mid 1980's and wasn't really mass produced until the First Gulf War when the British found themselves unable to properly clothe their personnel. This particular gear is the final in the series of DDPM.

Stunning and distinctive modern surplus from Great Britain. Issued to Royal Marine Commandos, it is designed for use in ceremonial occasions, it is akin to the army's No. 2 dress uniform, but with a few key distinctions. The jacket comes in a shade used only by the marines and features darkened bronze buttons which feature the emblem of the Royal Marines. 

The jacket has 4 external pockets, all of which can be buttoned shut and also features 2 internal slit pockets for smaller items. Shoulder epaulettes attach prestigious sashes and rank badges, along with other distinctive decorations. The jacket is lined with a sateen material and is made of a 100% quality wool material. Truly something special for those who do absolutely phenomenal work. 

For colour, "Lovat's Green" is a lovely blend of mossy greens and browns, a subtle combination that adds depth to a fantastic pair of trousers. This is likely as close as the British have to a "field grey" colour.

Beautiful elegant ceremonial dress from the British Army. This particular jacket from the British army would've been worn by a Warrant Officer on ceremonial duties, or for parade events. No. 1 dress is the highest level of dress uniform most soldiers will wear, and is earned after a good few years in the army, with each part of the uniform being tailor made.

For features, it is quite a simple jacket, made from 100% wool. There's 4 pockets in total, 2 flap and 2 buttonable flap pockets, arranged in the typical "safari" style, with 2 on the hips and 2 on the chest. The collar is mandarin style, being closed with 2 hook & eyes. On the shoulders you'll find shoulder epaulettes, usually designed to secure ribbons and other sashes during ceremonial events. For the colour, it is a very dark navy blue, bordering on black.

Overall great for a collector, especially given the niche branch, or reenactor, but also for costumes and reworking.

Given the Royal Signal Corps buttons it can be expected they would've been one of the first in action at the dissolution of Yugoslavia and would've been crucial to providing information to all other branches.

Vintage surplus that comes from the very early days of British DPM camouflage development. While not the first lot, it was still produced within the first decade or so of a nearly 50 year long refining process. Smocks like this one would go onto see use in the Falklands and the Troubles in Ireland. Designed to be worn by all personnel for combat use, it has plenty of maneuverability and storage.

Made from a very thick, durable cotton material the jacket is incredibly comfortable and soft for army surplus. It's almost entirely windproof and does a great job insulating, mainly thanks to the adjustable drawstrings, cuffs and the storm flap collar and front closure. If you've got the right layers on below, you'll be delightfully warm.

For practicalities, the smock has a great selection of pockets for storage. 4 Large ones are spread across the front body in the usual safari jacket style. On the shoulder there's a small button pocket for radios or tools and then internally, there's even more! If you carry soft or small items then the fishtail pouch and its other rear pockets will serve you well. 

Finally the jacket's colour is a very early colourway variant of DPM or Disruptive Pattern Material camouflage. This version, P68, has much lighter hues, with chocolates and light green colours, than the ones to follow after. DPM camouflage was tweaked for nearly 50 years, giving it quite the history.

Vintage surplus that comes from the very early days of British DPM camouflage development. While not the first lot, it was still produced within the first decade or so of a nearly 50 year long refining process. Smocks like this one would go onto see use in the Falklands and the Troubles in Ireland. Designed to be worn by all personnel for combat use, it has plenty of maneuverability and storage.

Made from a very thick, durable cotton material the jacket is incredibly comfortable and soft for army surplus. It's almost entirely windproof and does a great job insulating, mainly thanks to the adjustable drawstrings, cuffs and the storm flap collar and front closure. If you've got the right layers on below, you'll be delightfully warm.

For practicalities, the smock has a great selection of pockets for storage. 4 Large ones are spread across the front body in the usual safari jacket style. On the shoulder there's a small button pocket for radios or tools and then internally, there's even more! If you carry soft or small items then the fishtail pouch and its other rear pockets will serve you well. 

Finally the jacket's colour is a very early colourway variant of DPM or Disruptive Pattern Material camouflage. This version, P68, has much lighter hues, with chocolates and light green colours, than the ones to follow after. DPM camouflage was tweaked for nearly 50 years, giving it quite the history.

    A classic piece of surplus Great Britain. These lovely shirts were issued for a little over a decade and saw use in Iraq and the Gulf War. Made of a light poly-cotton material the shirt provides comfort and flexibility where needed. Officially these are combat jackets, but work just as well as a shirt!

    The jacket comes with 2 main chest pockets for storing slightly larger items and then a pen sleeve on the left with a small pocket on the right for whatever you may need. The jacket can be buttoned or zipped shut and if it's a particularly windy day the cuffs can be fastened tighter and collar overturned to provide better insulation.

    Desert Disruptive Pattern Material or DDPM, was developed in the mid 1980's and wasn't really mass produced until the First Gulf War when the British found themselves unable to properly clothe their personnel. This particular gear is the final in the series of DDPM.

A classic piece of world renowned surplus. This combat smock was issued during several UN missions which involved British peacekeeping forces during the fragmentation of Yugoslavia and was made just prior to the even more renowned S95 series of uniform. The 84 Pattern saw limited use before more modern materials became available, but the thick all cotton material still holds up today.

The smock offers ample storage, boasting 5 pockets as well as an internal "fishtail" pouch for storing softer items, a great feature when camping. In harsh conditions the coat can be drawn in at both the hem and waist, in addition to tightening the cuffs and zipping the collar right up. 

Of course the camouflage is the iconic woodland DPM pattern, a world renowned camo which still sees active use in 40+ countries, with many more using it prior. It's fantastic in temperate environments if you're looking for concealment, or stylish when worn casually.

A classic piece of world renowned surplus. This combat smock was issued during several UN missions which involved British peacekeeping forces during the fragmentation of Yugoslavia and was made just prior to the even more renowned S95 series of uniform. The 84 Pattern saw limited use before more modern materials became available, but the thick all cotton material still holds up today.

The smock offers ample storage, boasting 5 pockets as well as an internal "fishtail" pouch for storing softer items, a great feature when camping. In harsh conditions the coat can be drawn in at both the hem and waist, in addition to tightening the cuffs and zipping the collar right up. 

Of course the camouflage is the iconic woodland DPM pattern, a world renowned camo which still sees active use in 40+ countries, with many more using it prior. It's fantastic in temperate environments if you're looking for concealment, or stylish when worn casually.

Beautiful elegant ceremonial dress from the British Army. This particular jacket from the British army would've been worn by a Warrant Officer on ceremonial duties, or for parade events. No. 1 dress is the highest level of dress uniform most soldiers will wear, and is earned after a good few years in the army, with each part of the uniform being tailor made.

For features, it is quite a simple jacket, made from 100% wool. There's 4 pockets in total, 2 flap and 2 buttonable flap pockets, arranged in the typical "safari" style, with 2 on the hips and 2 on the chest. The collar is mandarin style, being closed with 2 hook & eyes. On the shoulders you'll find shoulder epaulettes, usually designed to secure ribbons and other sashes during ceremonial events. For the colour, it is a very dark navy blue, bordering on black.

Overall great for a collector, especially given the niche branch, or reenactor, but also for costumes and reworking.

A classic piece of world renowned surplus. This combat smock was issued during several UN missions which involved British peacekeeping forces during the fragmentation of Yugoslavia and was made just prior to the even more renowned S95 series of uniform. The 84 Pattern saw limited use before more modern materials became available, but the thick all cotton material still holds up today.

The smock offers ample storage, boasting 5 pockets as well as an internal "fishtail" pouch for storing softer items, a great feature when camping. In harsh conditions the coat can be drawn in at both the hem and waist, in addition to tightening the cuffs and zipping the collar right up. 

Of course the camouflage is the iconic woodland DPM pattern, a world renowned camo which still sees active use in 40+ countries, with many more using it prior. It's fantastic in temperate environments if you're looking for concealment, or stylish when worn casually.

title: British Air Force RAF 72 Pattern GP Jacket - Royal Observer Corps - Large 180/108
body_html:
At a glance - 

  • 100% Wool Material
  • 2 Zipper Chest Pockets
  • Zipper Closure
  • Shoulder Epaulettes
  • "Royal Observer Corps 22" Shoulder Patches
  • Royal Observer Corps Medal Ribbon Bar
  • Classic Air Force Blue Colour
  • "JACKET MANS, blue grey, 1972 Pattern"
  • Pit to Pit: 23" | Suggested Size: Large Slim - Label suggests a chest around 108cm
  • Sleeve Length: 26" / Long - Label recommends a height around 180cm
  • Collar to Hem: 26"
  • Vintage Militaria / 1972 - 1979
  • Genuine British Royal Air Force / RAF Surplus

Grades - 

  • Grade 1 - In great shape for its age. Some general signs of prior use but up for much more

Any questions please feel free to ask!

- - - - - - -

A fantastic jacket with a rich history from a gentleman who was based in West Wales. Having served in the Second World War, he served in active duty over France & Germany late into the war with the Royal Observer Corps, which as the name suggests was an observation branch of the British Forces crucial to providing intelligence and strategy to the allies' offensive. After his service he kept up with army life by transferring to the reserves where he taught in the local Air Cadet's branch, sharing his plethora of knowledge. 

The jacket itself is the precursor to the now well known GP bomber jacket. This older 1972 pattern design is cut in a style fitting to the time, with 2 slanted zipper pockets for storage and a front zipper closure. It is made of an all wool material in the beautiful RAF blue colour. The wool of course offering wind and water resistance in the middling to summer months. The jacket is a great piece of history without being exceptionally ornate as the stunning dress jackets usually are, but certainly showcase well a rich life in the field.

A classic piece of vintage British surplus. This jacket is the predecessor to the current issued No. 2 uniform, which takes much of its inspiration from this beautiful jacket which in turn has been formed from hundreds of years of military history. Jackets like this one were used for ceremonial and general duties around barracks and the likes. It is slightly more boxy than the newer issued jackets, but is of fantastic quality.

The jacket has a sophisticated yet utilitarian look, made with purpose. It has 2 chest pockets along with 2 much larger flap hip pockets, as well as internal slit pockets for storing important or smaller items, everything from IDs and wallets to packets of gum and cigarettes.

This particular jacket belonged to an individual who had a lengthy career in the army, seeing conflict in Yugoslavia and her remnants. At one point there were rank patches that appear to have fitted the rank of Sergeant but these have been removed. Given the Royal Signal Corps buttons it can be expected they would've been one of the first in action at the dissolution of Yugoslavia and would've been crucial to providing information to all other branches.

Classic surplus from the British Army. These trousers were "standard" issue in the scramble to fully equip the British Army for arid, desert terrains in light of the First Gulf War. The more famous, S95 series issued from 1995 onwards, of desert trouser didn't change all too much when building off the original design that these trousers used. This older pair has more conventional buttons, a thicker cotton material and a slightly different camouflage pattern.

- - - - - - -

Vintage surplus that comes from the very early days of British DPM camouflage development. While not the first lot, it was still produced within the first decade or so of a nearly 50 year long refining process. Smocks like this one would go onto see use in the Falklands and the Troubles in Ireland. Designed to be worn by all personnel for combat use, it has plenty of maneuverability and storage.

Made from a very thick, durable cotton material the jacket is incredibly comfortable and soft for army surplus. It's almost entirely windproof and does a great job insulating, mainly thanks to the adjustable drawstrings, cuffs and the storm flap collar and front closure. If you've got the right layers on below, you'll be delightfully warm.

For practicalities, the smock has a great selection of pockets for storage. 4 Large ones are spread across the front body in the usual safari jacket style. On the shoulder there's a small button pocket for radios or tools and then internally, there's even more! If you carry soft or small items then the fishtail pouch and its other rear pockets will serve you well. 

Finally the jacket's colour is a very early colourway variant of DPM or Disruptive Pattern Material camouflage. Any questions please feel free to ask!

- - - - - - -

Classic surplus from the British Army. These trousers were "standard" issue in the scramble to fully equip the British Army for arid, desert terrains in light of the First Gulf War. The more famous, S95 series issued from 1995 onwards, of desert trouser didn't change all too much when building off the original design that these trousers used. This older pair has more conventional buttons, a thicker cotton material and a slightly different camouflage pattern. 

The trousers come with 2 large cargo pockets as well as 2 regular waist / hip pockets for all of your lightweight storage needs. To provide a more tailored fit, you'll find not only a 2" belt loop system for attaching things like duty and pistol belts, but also a drawstring around the waist and each trouser cuff. The side of the waistband can also be tightened via buttons if desired.

As for the camouflage pattern, the Desert DPM design is world renowned and has gone onto inspire hundreds of camouflage designs, from Britain's allies to her enemies as well as designer brands. These trousers utilise the lightly lighter and sandier colourway which was later adjusted in the S95 range. Over all a great pair of trousers for casual wear or hiking and bushcraft.

A quintessential part of British army memorabilia. Reserved for those who have a long serving history in the Forces, who guard Buckingham Palace, this greatcoat is made of a high quality all wool material and comes with a unique and timeless design.

The coat comes with a tall funnel neck collar which can be overturned and fastened in harsh winds and cold winter weather. There's 2 deep flap pockets on the waist offering ample storage. Each button is engraved which adds a lovely bit of character. It comes in a solid grey colour which has a purple tint. 

It's a stunning, stylish garment that is a fantastic statement piece for casual use or for a reenactor or theatre groups. Being so iconic from the front gates of Buckingham Palace, you can imagine the versatility these coats would have in any like minded wardrobe. 

And as a helpful tip, you can just look at the Foot Guard's uniform to tell which time the UK is currently using. Red tunics for British Summer Time and these greatcoats for Greenwich Mean Time. So if you're in the area and confused about when daylight savings is happening, just take a look at the Guards.

Beautiful ceremonial surplus from modern day Great Britain. Used exclusively for ceremonial and official duties, Since such occasions are a rarity, so is the construct quality of these trousers. Made to the highest specifications for the British army, of the finest wool. These trousers see use namely by the footguards as stated on the inner label but also musicians, sergeants, and a few others.

The trousers are beautifully made and feature a wing tipped rear, a button fly and 2 decent sized waist pockets. The cuffs are slightly slanted as is the official style. Really a fantastic piece of surplus that carries plenty of heritage just in style alone.

Stunning and bold surplus from the Royal Hussars. This British surplus is worn as a walking out dress piece for the Royal Hussars and is their unique take on the standard No. 2 dress uniform. It does feature much of the usual No. 2  design but is in a distinct crimson / burgundy colour which sets it apart from the rest.

For features you'll find 2 front waist pockets and 2 rear pockets. The trousers offer 2" belt loops or as worn by officer's internal suspender buttons. The waistband is fastened with a zipper and hook & eye closure. Each trouser leg is beautifully pleated front and back making for a timeless look even in a more unusual style.

The coat comes with a tall funnel neck collar which can be overturned and fastened in harsh winds and cold winter weather. There's 2 deep flap pockets on the waist offering ample storage. It's a stunning, stylish garment that is a fantastic statement piece for casual use or for a reenactor or theatre groups. Being so iconic from the front gates of Buckingham Palace, you can imagine the versatility these coats would have in any like minded wardrobe.

Beautiful ceremonial surplus from modern day Great Britain. Used exclusively for ceremonial and official duties, Since such occasions are a rarity, so is the construct quality of these trousers. Made to the highest specifications for the British army, of the finest wool. These trousers see use namely by the footguards as stated on the inner label but also musicians, sergeants, and a few others.

The trousers are beautifully made and feature a wing tipped rear, a button fly and 2 decent sized waist pockets. The cuffs are slightly slanted as is the official style. The scarlet red piping is continuous on both legs. The trousers are designed to be worn with suspenders and as such you'll find several buttons on the inner waist hem. Really a fantastic piece of surplus that carries plenty of heritage just in style alone.

Stunning and bold surplus from the Royal Hussars. This British surplus is worn as a walking out dress piece for the Royal Hussars and is their unique take on the standard No. 2 dress uniform. It does feature much of the usual No. 2  design but is in a distinct crimson / burgundy colour which sets it apart from the rest.

For features you'll find 2 front waist pockets and 2 rear pockets. The trousers offer 2" belt loops or as worn by officer's internal suspender buttons. The waistband is fastened with a zipper and hook & eye closure. Each trouser leg is beautifully pleated front and back making for a timeless look even in a more unusual style.

A quintessential part of British army memorabilia. Reserved for those who have a long serving history in the Forces, who guard Buckingham Palace, this greatcoat is made of a high quality all wool material and comes with a unique and timeless design.

The coat comes with a tall funnel neck collar which can be overturned and fastened in harsh winds and cold winter weather. There's 2 deep flap pockets on the waist offering ample storage. Each button is engraved which adds a lovely bit of character. It comes in a solid grey colour which has a purple tint. 

It's a stunning, stylish garment that is a fantastic statement piece for casual use or for a reenactor or theatre groups. Being so iconic from the front gates of Buckingham Palace, you can imagine the versatility these coats would have in any like minded wardrobe. 

And as a helpful tip, you can just look at the Foot Guard's uniform to tell which time the UK is currently using. Red tunics for British Summer Time and these greatcoats for Greenwich Mean Time. So if you're in the area and confused about when daylight savings is happening, just take a look at the Guards.

    Brilliant tactical surplus from the modern British Army. This currently issued standard piece of kit is a wonderful staple of the British Armed Forces, often seeing action across the board in a whole range of environments, from grassy plains to heathered hillsides and mountain ranges.

    The smock comes with a total 10 pockets, all of which can be fastened shut, offering plenty of options for storage. On harsher days the "handwarmer" pockets are a delight. Another great feature for blustery weather is the drawstring around the hood and hem, combine that with the adjustable cuffs and you can insulate yourself wonderfully within this jacket. 

    As for the camouflage pattern, it is of course British MTP or "Multi Terrain Pattern" camouflage, which takes the pattern design from the old British DPM camouflage and blends it with the colours and hues of the American "Multicam" camouflage for one fantastically effective lovechild.

A classic piece of world renowned surplus. This combat smock was issued during several UN missions which involved British peacekeeping forces during the fragmentation of Yugoslavia and was made just prior to the even more renowned S95 series of uniform. The 84 Pattern saw limited use before more modern materials became available, but the thick all cotton material still holds up today.

The smock offers ample storage, boasting 5 pockets as well as an internal "fishtail" pouch for storing softer items, a great feature when camping. In harsh conditions the coat can be drawn in at both the hem and waist, in addition to tightening the cuffs and zipping the collar right up. 

Of course the camouflage is the iconic woodland DPM pattern, a world renowned camo which still sees active use in 40+ countries, with many more using it prior. It's fantastic in temperate environments if you're looking for concealment, or stylish when worn casually.

Beautiful elegant ceremonial dress from the British Army. This particular jacket from the British army would've been worn for ceremonial duties, or for parade events. No. 1 dress is the highest level of dress uniform most soldiers will wear, and is earned after a good few years in the army, with each part of the uniform being tailor made.

For features, it is quite a simple jacket, made from 100% wool. There's 4 pockets in total, 2 flap and 2 buttonable flap pockets, arranged in the typical "safari" style, with 2 on the hips and 2 on the chest. The collar is mandarin style, being closed with 2 hook & eyes. On the shoulders you'll find shoulder epaulettes, usually designed to secure ribbons and other sashes during ceremonial events. For the colour, it is a very dark navy blue, bordering on black.

A quintessential part of British army memorabilia. Reserved for those who have a long serving history in the Forces, who guard Buckingham Palace, this greatcoat is made of a high quality all wool material and comes with a unique and timeless design.

The coat comes with a tall funnel neck collar which can be overturned and fastened in harsh winds and cold winter weather. There's 2 deep flap pockets on the waist offering ample storage. Each button is engraved which adds a lovely bit of character. It comes in a solid grey colour which has a purple tint. 

It's a stunning, stylish garment that is a fantastic statement piece for casual use or for a reenactor or theatre groups. Being so iconic from the front gates of Buckingham Palace, you can imagine the versatility these coats would have in any like minded wardrobe. 

And as a helpful tip, you can just look at the Foot Guard's uniform to tell which time the UK is currently using. Red tunics for British Summer Time and these greatcoats for Greenwich Mean Time. So if you're in the area and confused about when daylight savings is happening, just take a look at the Guards.

A classic piece of vintage British surplus. This jacket is the predecessor to the current issued No. 2 uniform, which takes much of its inspiration from this beautiful jacket which in turn has been formed from hundreds of years of military history. Jackets like this one were used for ceremonial and general duties around barracks and the likes. It is slightly more boxy than the newer issued jackets, but is of fantastic quality.

The jacket has a sophisticated yet utilitarian look, made with purpose. It has 2 chest pockets along with 2 much larger flap hip pockets, as well as internal slit pockets for storing important or smaller items, everything from IDs and wallets to packets of gum and cigarettes.

This particular jacket belonged to an individual who had a lengthy career in the army, seeing conflict in Yugoslavia and her remnants. At one point there were rank patches that appear to have fitted the rank of Sergeant but these have been removed. Given the Royal Signal Corps buttons it can be expected they would've been one of the first in action at the dissolution of Yugoslavia and would've been crucial to providing information to all other branches.

We often have a few old pattern No. 2 dress trousers on hand if you're after a complete uniform!

Classic surplus from the British Army. These trousers were "standard" issue in the scramble to fully equip the British Army for arid, desert terrains in light of the First Gulf War. The more famous, S95 series issued from 1995 onwards, of desert trouser didn't change all too much when building off the original design that these trousers used. This older pair has more conventional buttons, a thicker cotton material and a slightly different camouflage pattern. 

The trousers come with 2 large cargo pockets as well as 2 regular waist / hip pockets for all of your lightweight storage needs. To provide a more tailored fit, you'll find not only a 2" belt loop system for attaching things like duty and pistol belts, but also a drawstring around the waist and each trouser cuff. The side of the waistband can also be tightened via buttons if desired.

As for the camouflage pattern, the Desert DPM design is world renowned and has gone onto inspire hundreds of camouflage designs, from Britain's allies to her enemies as well as designer brands. These trousers utilise the lightly lighter and sandier colourway which was later adjusted in the S95 range. Over all a great pair of trousers for casual wear or hiking and bushcraft.

Retro British surplus that has been around for quite a few decades. Seeing use with several British peace keeping forces, UN operations and just general garrison duty in warmer climates and old colonies, they're a pretty nifty shirt! They're also made of a light poly-cotton blend, so they're a comfortable fit, great for warmer months!

The No. 9 uniform is quite interesting for its various colour shades, despite technically being classed as the exact same uniform, due to several tweaks over the years of manufacture. Retro British surplus that has been around for quite a few decades. Seeing use with several British peace keeping forces, UN operations and just general garrison duty in warmer climates and old colonies, they're a pretty nifty shirt! They're also made of a light poly-cotton blend, so they're a comfortable fit, great for warmer months!

The No.9 uniform is quite interesting for its various colour shades, despite technically being classed as the exact same uniform, due to several tweaks over the years of manufacture. From it's initial production around 1974, the colours changed drastically from light, airy hues to the darker and more iconic DPM pattern we know today.

The shirt listed here were produced around the early 1980s and use a pretty light colourway. They also use the old British size charts, with "Size 1" labelled inside rather than the NATO friendly current labels.

In 2011 the British army swapped over to a new type of standardized uniform and the No.9 tropical combat uniform was made obsolete. It's a great shirt, especially with the more distinct, characterful choice of buttons and colours than the newer kit!

We often stock the later versions, which are much closer to the known S95 DPM camouflage, with darker, saturated greens and deep browns.

Vintage militaria from the early 90's. This British combat smock would've seen use during various UN peacekeeping missions as it was standard issue. This jacket comes in the last pattern before the modern made Soldier 95 series, which revolutionised the British army's uniform system with one standardised, effect garment. Still, this coat served many soldiers well and is made from a durable all cotton material.

It appears the previous owner added a keen hand at sewing and added an extra internal pouch. By default you'll find 4 spacious button pockets, 2 chest and 2 hip, as well as a handy little pocket on each sleeve. Internally there's a large "fishtail" pocket for storing soft goods like sleeping mats, clothing etc. 

For utility you'll find the collar can be overturned and fastened shut in harsh conditions and each sleeve cuff is able to be velcro'd tight. There's a hem and waist drawstring so you can really help insulate yourself in cold windy weather.

The camouflage is of course the iconic woodland DPM pattern, a world renowned camo which still sees active use in 40+ countries.
